sections.html:
Alabama taxes come due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31. After that the file goes to the probate court in February, the court meets in March, the property is advertised in April, and the tax sale happens in May.

MonthStage of the delinquent account
October 1Taxes due
January 1Taxes delinquent
FebruaryTurned over to probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilAdvertised for sale
MayTax sale

That calendar describes the traditional property sale. Some counties now use a different remedy, covered below, so treat the months as a guide and call your county's collection office for the actual dates on your parcel.

sections.h2: Who can redeem, and for how long
sections.html:
Redemption rules are in Alabama Code section 40-10-120. When the state bought the land, it can be redeemed at any point before title leaves the state. When anyone else bought it, you have three years from the sale date.

A wide group may redeem:

  • The owner, the owner's heirs or personal representatives.
  • A mortgagee, or a purchaser of all or part of the land.
  • Anyone with a legal or equitable interest, a tenant in common included.
  • A judgment creditor or other creditor holding a lien.

A minor or legally incompetent person gets one year after the disability ends, even if the three years have run out. A mortgage or lien properly recorded at the time of the sale carries an added right: its holder can redeem within one year from the date written notice of the purchase is served.

You may redeem part of the land sold as long as the payment covers your whole interest. And if the same land was sold again in later tax sales, redeeming the first sale means redeeming the later ones at the same time.

Apply to the county probate judge and deposit the price the land sold for, eight percent interest on it, every tax found due since the sale with eight percent interest, and officer costs and fees. Section 40-10-121 sets this out.

The state never paid the later years of tax, so the county assessor writes an assessed value for each year since the sale onto your application. If you disagree, file a written protest with the board of equalization. It schedules a hearing after at least 10 days of written notice and sends the value it fixes to the probate judge.

When any of the land lies inside a municipality, you also deposit the municipality's unpaid taxes plus the municipal tax that went unassessed while the state held the land, with the interest that would have built up. Owners often miss this item when they estimate a payoff.

sections.h2: Redeeming land a private buyer bought
sections.html:
For sales to someone other than the state, section 40-10-122 applies. You deposit with the probate judge the sale price plus eight percent interest per annum from the sale date, and on the part of any excess bid that is 15 percent of assessed market value or less. Add any taxes the purchaser paid, with eight percent interest.

If taxes assessed to the purchaser are still unpaid, pay those to the tax collector before you redeem. You also pay officer costs and fees and a $0.50 fee to the probate judge, and the application and payment can be made online.

Houses add more. If a residential structure stood on the land at the time of sale, you must reimburse the purchaser's casualty insurance premiums, paid or owed, and the value of preservation improvements, each with eight percent interest. Preservation improvements are work done to keep the property in proper repair. Valuing them follows a short routine:

  1. Make a written demand for a statement of improvement value.
  2. The purchaser has 10 days to answer with a figure.
  3. You have 10 days to accept it or name a referee.
  4. Referees confer, and if they can't agree they choose an umpire. The majority award is final between the parties.

You can take possession before paying the improvement and insurance amounts, but you must reimburse them before January 1 of the following tax year or the right in the property is lost.

sections.h2: Do all counties still sell the property?
sections.html:
No. Act 2018-577 let tax collecting officials sell a tax lien in place of the property. Baldwin County's Revenue Commission moved to lien sales beginning in 2019 with tax year 2018 delinquent properties, and every lien for unpaid real property tax there goes to public auction. Bidders use the GovEase platform through the county's tax lien auction page.

For an owner the questions stay the same: how much is owed, who holds the claim, how much time is left, and what it costs to clear. A lien sale and a property sale do need different paperwork, though, so ask your county revenue office which remedy covers your parcel.

Baldwin is one example of the lien route. Other counties may still run the traditional sale, so don't assume the rules match from county to county.

sections.h2: Recording and redemption in Jefferson County
sections.html:
The Jefferson County probate court takes documents at two locations. The Birmingham division is in the Jefferson County Courthouse at 716 North Richard Arrington Jr. Blvd., and the Bessemer division is at 1801 3rd Avenue North in Bessemer. Recording hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.

The recording office can't run a title search and can't prepare or revise a deed. For lien searches and legal paperwork, use a title company or attorney. Redemption deposits go to the probate judge, so a call to your own county's probate office is the best first step for exact amounts.

sections.h2: How a pending tax sale affects your sale
sections.html:
You can usually sell ahead of the tax sale or during redemption if the buyer, or the buyer's title company, pays what's owed from the proceeds. The delinquent tax, interest and any redemption deposit show up as lines on the settlement statement.

Gather these before you talk to a buyer:

  • The parcel number and each delinquent tax year.
  • Whether the county sold the property or a lien, and the date.
  • The purchaser: the state or a private buyer.
  • A payoff figure from the probate judge or tax collector.
  • Any mortgage or lien holders, who may hold their own redemption window.

Time works against you. Three years for a private purchase sounds generous, but eight percent interest runs the whole stretch, and improvements and insurance paid by the purchaser on a house raise the payoff further. An as-is cash sale can clear the redemption amount at closing with no repairs or showings in the way.

faqs.q: When do Alabama property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: Taxes are due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31. The delinquent file then goes to probate court in February, with a tax sale in May.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Three years from the sale date if a private buyer bought the property. If the state bought it, you can redeem any time before title leaves the state.

faqs.q: What interest rate applies to redemption?
faqs.a: Eight percent. Sections 40-10-121 and 40-10-122 both use it on the sale price and on the other amounts the redeeming party owes.

faqs.q: Who do I pay to redeem?
faqs.a: The judge of probate in the county where the land sits. Section 40-10-122 also allows the application and payment to be made online.

faqs.q: Can I sell to a cash buyer before the sale or during redemption?
faqs.a: Often yes, if the amount owed can be paid from the proceeds and title can be delivered. Get a payoff figure first, and ask an Alabama attorney if a mortgage holder or other lienholder is involved.
